query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating microstructural defect information and oxygen impurity effects into a predictive, data‐driven electrical conductivity model will yield more accurate conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes than conventional perfect-crystal analytical models.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr synthesized via powder metallurgy or spark plasma sintering (SPS) from gas-atomized powders, with one set having very low oxygen content and a second specimen intentionally containing ~1 wt.% oxygen.
generation.intervention: Augment existing analytical models by incorporating parameters that account for grain boundary networks, dislocation densities, and oxygen-induced lattice distortions, using inputs from ab initio-based data and active learning strategies.
generation.conditions: Electrical conductivity measurements performed at 0–200 K (where quantum and scattering effects are prominent) and at 300–1200 K (covering high-temperature behavior) on samples with and without ~1 wt.% oxygen.
generation.structural_mediator: Microstructural features including grain boundaries, defect densities, and oxygen-related defect complexes that modulate electron scattering and thus impact conductivity.
generation.mechanism: Oxygen impurities and processing-induced defects cause local lattice distortions, which in turn alter the electron scattering rates and mobility. By explicitly incorporating these effects into the predictive model, the approach overcomes the limited accuracy of models that assume defect-free crystals.
generation.predicted_outcome: The predictive model will yield conductivity values that more closely match measured data across the two temperature regimes, correctly predicting lower temperature sensitivity due to defect-induced scattering and improved agreement for oxygen-containing specimens compared with traditional models.
generation.baseline: Standard analytical conductivity predictions based on perfect, defect-free hcp or bcc crystal approximations, which inadequately capture the impact of real microstructural defects and oxygen impurities.
generation.boundary: The approach is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr produced under similar processing conditions (e.g., SPS or powder metallurgy) and for oxygen contents up to ~1 wt.%; predictions may deviate for temperatures above 1200 K where additional phase instabilities could play a role.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain if all key defect types and oxygen-induced effects, particularly at the very low temperature regime (0–200 K), can be fully captured by the augmented model. Further, high-temperature (above 1200 K) behavior might be influenced by phase changes not considered in the model.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples: one with minimal oxygen (<0.1 wt.%) and one with ~1 wt.% oxygen. Carry out electrical conductivity measurements across both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes. Compare the outcomes with predictions from both the enhanced predictive model and the traditional perfect-crystal model.
measurements: Characterization of microstructural features (grain boundary density, defect distribution) via microscopy techniques
Oxygen content analysis using, e.g., electron-probe microanalysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the enhanced predictive approach does not yield statistically significant improvements in conductivity prediction accuracy over traditional models across the tested temperature ranges, or if experimental trends do not exhibit the predicted sensitivity to 1 wt.% oxygen and corresponding defect structures.

## Abstract
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) provide new research avenues for alloy combinations in the periodic table, opening numerous possibilities in novel-alloy applications. However, their electrical characteristics have been relatively underexplored. The challenge in establishing an HEA electrical conductivity model lies in the changes in electronic characteristics caused by lattice distortion and complexity of nanostructures. Here we show a low-frequency electrical conductivity model for the Nb-Mo-Ta-W HEA system. The cocktail effect is found to explain trends in electrical-conductivity changes in HEAs, while the magnitude of the reduction is understood by the calculated plasma frequency, free electron density, and measured relaxation time by terahertz spectroscopy. As a result, the refractory HEA Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 thin film exhibits both high hardness and excellent conductivity. This combination of Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 makes it suitable for applications in atomic force microscopy probe coating, significantly improving their wear resistance and atomic-scale image resolution. ## Abstract
AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEA) have been one of the most attractive groups of materials for researchers in the last several years. Since HEAs are potential candidates for many (e.g., refractory, cryogenic, medical) applications, their properties are studied intensively. The most frequent method of HEA synthesis is arc or induction melting. Powder metallurgy is a perspective technique of alloy synthesis and therefore in this work the possibilities of synthesis of HfNbTaTiZr HEA from powders were studied. Blended elemental powders were sintered, hot isostatically pressed, and subsequently swaged using a special technique of swaging where the sample is enveloped by a titanium alloy. This method does not result in a full density alloy due to cracking during swaging. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed powders resulted in a fully dense but brittle specimen. The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content.
